To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

two different types of neurons in frontal eye field (FEF) are involved in saccade selection: (1) a subset of neurons initially selects the target, and (2) the remaining neurons select the saccade endpoint.
the neural selection of the visual target is independent of the response type (prosaccade vs. antisaccade), but the neural selection of saccade endpoint is affected by the response type.
the time of visual selection is not affected by stimulus–response compatibility and is not correlated with reaction time, while the time of saccade selection is correlated with reaction time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain selects a single object from a group of visual objects and how it selects the saccade that will bring the object into view.
the mechanisms that allow the brain to select the correct action to perform in response to a given stimulus, and the way in which the brain selects between different possible actions.
understanding the neural basis of the selection processes involved in visual search.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
visual selection and motor selection are different processes and are mediated by different neuronal populations.
there are at least three types of neurons in the FEF, which are involved in different aspects of visual and s accade selection.
the FEF is not involved in the selection of visual targets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are two types of neurons in frontal eye field: one that encodes the location of visual stimulus and another that encodes the goal of saccade.
visual attention and saccade preparation are different processes, and that visual attention is not necessary for the preparation of a saccade, although visual selection may affect reaction time.
the frontal eye field (FEF) is involved in the selection of saccade targets and that the selection of sakkadic targets is independent of the selection of visual objects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the selection of the saccadic endpoint is the main factor determining the effect of stimulus response compatibility on reaction time in the frontal eye fields.
the neural selection of a saccade endpoint in frontal eye field is affected by stimulus-response congruity.
the time of selection of a saccade goal is the main determinant of saccade reaction time, and that this selection is affected by stimulus-response (S-R) compatibility.
